# Question 1: Sea Surface Temperature modelling

## a) Plot and comment on the data

```{r,warning=FALSE,message=FALSE}
# load the dataset
SST <- read.csv("D:/Bureau/University of Exeter UK/Modules/Data Science and Statistical Modelling in Space and Time/Coursework/kuroshio100.csv",
                header = T,sep = ',',dec = '.')

head(SST,n=5)

# check for missing values
colSums(is.na(SST))
```

```{r,warning=FALSE,message=FALSE,cache=TRUE,results='hide'}
# imputation of the NA by using mean function
# Remove rows with missing coordinates
library(tidyverse)
SST_clean <- SST %>% drop_na(lon, lat)

# impute sst and at variables

# Select variables to impute
vars_to_impute <- SST_clean %>% 
  select(sst, at)  # include all with NA (not lon/lat)

# Run mice
library(mice)
# method = 'pmm': Predictive Mean Matching, safe for numeric data
imp <- mice(vars_to_impute, m = 5, method = 'pmm', seed = 123)

# Complete the dataset with the first imputation
imputed_vars <- complete(imp, 1)

# Add imputed values back to the cleaned data
SST_imputed <- SST_clean %>%
  select(-sst, -at) %>%
  bind_cols(imputed_vars)

```

```{r,warning=FALSE,message=FALSE,cache=TRUE}
library(geoR) 
# Check duplicated coordinates
dup_locations <- dup.coords(SST_imputed[, c("lon", "lat")])
#print(dup_locations)

# Apply jitter to duplicated coordinates
sst_coords <- jitterDupCoords(SST_imputed[, c("lon", "lat")], max = 0.0001)

# Create a new data frame with jittered coords and original temperature values
SST_jittered <- data.frame(
  lon = sst_coords[, 1],
  lat = sst_coords[, 2],
  sst = SST_imputed$sst,
  date = SST_imputed$date,
  id = SST_imputed$id,
  pt = SST_imputed$pt,
  sf = SST_imputed$sf,
  at = SST_imputed$at,
  af = SST_imputed$af
  
)

colSums(is.na(SST_imputed))
```

```{r,warning=FALSE,message=FALSE,cache=TRUE,fig.cap='Spatial plots',fig-plot1}
library(geoR)      # for geostatistics and as.geodata
library(ggplot2)   # for nice plots
library(tidyverse) # for data manipulation

##  convert the data into a geodata object 
sst_geo1 <- as.geodata(SST_jittered, coords.col = c("lon", "lat"), 
                      data.col = "sst")


# spatial plot
plot(sst_geo1, main.title = "Sea Surface Temperature (SST)")

```

## Comments

The top left figure shows spatial distribution by groups (@fig-plot1). Different colours and shapes (blue circles, green triangles, red crosses, yellow pluses) represent distinct groups or clusters. There appears to be spatial clustering. For instance, the blue group is concentrated in the north region, while red and yellow are more southward. The green one is well distributed in the region. The top right panel exhibits the Sea Surface Temperature (SST) alongside the latitude. There is a negative trend. The SST decreases as the latitude increases. The bottom left panel shows that there is no significant trend between the Sea surface temperature and the longitude. Its values are spread across longitudes, especially around 142-146°. The histogram and density plot reveal the SST is not normally distributed. There is presence of multimodality, implying spatially distinct temperature regimes.

## (c) Spatial model fitting using the variogram/kriging approach

```{r,warning=FALSE,message=FALSE,cache=TRUE,fig.cap='Sample Variograms',fig-plot2}

##  convert the data into a geodata object 
sst_geo <- as.geodata(train_data, coords.col = c("lon", "lat"), 
                      data.col = "sst")



library(geoR)
par(mfrow=c(3,2),mar=c(4,4,2,2))

# Variogram plot without setting maximum distance with trend = cte
sample_vario.cte <- variog(sst_geo, option='bin',trend = 'cte')
plot(sample_vario.cte, main = "Sample Variogram with Trend Constante",
     pch=19)

# Variogram plot with 1st trend = 1st
sample_vario.trend1 <- variog(sst_geo, option='bin',trend = '1st')
plot(sample_vario.trend1, main = "Empirical Variogram with Trend 1st",
     pch=19)

# Variogram plot with trend = 2nd
sample_vario.trend2 <- variog(sst_geo, option='bin',trend = '2nd')
plot(sample_vario.trend2, main = "Empirical Variogram with Trend 2nd",
     pch=19)
```

## Comments

The three sample variograms (@fig-plot2) presented show the spatial structure of the data under different trend assumptions: constant, first-order, and second-order. In the variogram with a constant trend, the semi-variance increases with distance and does not appear to reach a clear sill within the plotted range. This suggests the presence of spatial autocorrelation over long distances and indicates the need to set a maximum distance (cut-off) at 10 to avoid unstable variogram fitting at large distances where few point pairs exist. Moreover, the jump at the origin suggests the presence of a nugget effect, which may capture measurement error or microscale variability.

In contrast, the variogram under the first-order trend is flatter and reaches a sill more clearly, indicating that some of the spatial structure has been explained by the trend component. The presence of a nugget is still apparent due to the semi-variance not starting at zero, and it should be included in the model. The second-order trend variogram appears even flatter, with very little increase in semi-variance over distance, implying that most of the spatial trend has been removed and that the residuals have weak spatial autocorrelation. However, a nugget effect still seems to be present. Thus, including a nugget in all models is appropriate, and setting a reasonable maximum distance at 10 is advisable, especially in the constant trend case, to improve variogram stability.

#### Variogram Approach

**Constant trend model** **assumptions**

1.  Trend/Mean Function

we assume a constant mean function, also known as a zero-order polynomial trend.

This means that the spatial process has a constant average value across the spatial domain:

$$
\mu(s) = \beta_0
$$

where:

-   $\mu(s)$ is the spatial mean at location $s$,

-   $\beta_0$ is the intercept (constant mean).

​This assumption is appropriate when there's no significant large-scale trend in the data or after detrending has been applied.

2.  Covariance Function

We use the exponential covariance model, specified as:

$$
C(h) = \sigma^2 \exp\left(-\frac{h}{\phi}\right)
$$

-   $\sigma^2$ is the partial sill (spatial variance),

-   $\phi$ is the range parameter (how quickly correlation decays with distance).

The exponential model implies that spatial dependence decays rapidly with distance.

3.  Nugget Effect

A nugget effect is included to capture:

-   Measurement error or microscale variation.

-   A jump in the variogram at very short distances (as seen in the empirical variogram).

The total variogram is modelled as:

$$
\gamma(h) = \tau^2 + \sigma^2 \left(1 - \exp\left(-\frac{h}{\phi}\right)\right)
$$

where:

-   $\tau^2$ is the nugget effect (micro-scale variation and measurement error),
-   $\sigma^2$ is the partial sill (spatial variance),
-   $\phi$ is the range parameter (how quickly correlation reaches its maximum),
-   $\tau^2$ is the nugget.

**First and second-order polynomial trend assumptions**

1.  Trend/Mean Function

We assume a first-order polynomial trend (trend = '1st' or '2nd'), which means the mean of the spatial process is modelled as a linear function of spatial coordinates:

$$
\mu(s) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 y
$$

This accounts for large-scale spatial variation and trends in the data due to spatial drift or gradient.

2.  Covariance Function

We used the exponential covariance model, defined as:

$$
C(h) = \sigma^2 \exp\left(-\frac{h}{\phi}\right)
$$

where:

-   $h$ is the separation distance between locations,

-   $\sigma^2$ is the partial sill (spatially structured variance),

-   $\phi$ is the range parameter (distance over which points are correlated).

3.  Nugget Effect

We included a nugget effect in the model to account for:

-   Measurement error or microscale variation not captured by the spatial structure.

-   The discontinuity at the origin of the variogram.

This adds a discontinuous jump at distance $h=0$, modelled as:

$$
\gamma(h) = \tau^2 + \sigma^2 \left(1 - \exp\left(-\frac{h}{\phi}\right)\right)
$$

where:

-   $\tau^2$ is the nugget effect (micro-scale variation and measurement error),

-   $\sigma^2$ is the partial sill (spatial variance),

-   $\phi$ is the range parameter (how quickly correlation reaches its maximum),

-   $\tau^2$ is the nugget.

### Constant Trend Models

```{r,warning=FALSE,message=FALSE,cache=TRUE,results='hide'}

## Empirical variogram plots with maximum distance equal to 10
par(mfrow=c(3,2),mar=c(4,4,2,2))
sample_vario.dist.cte <- variog(sst_geo, option='bin',
                                trend = 'cte',max.dist = 10)
plot(sample_vario.dist.cte, 
     main = "Sample Variogram with Trend Constante",
     pch=19)

# Variogram plot with 1st trend = 1st
sample_vario.dist.trend1 <- variog(sst_geo, option='bin',
                                   trend = '1st',max.dist = 10)
plot(sample_vario.dist.trend1, 
     main = "Empirical Variogram with Trend 1st",
     pch=19)

# Variogram plot with trend = 2nd
sample_vario.dist.trend2 <- variog(sst_geo, option='bin',
                                   trend = '2nd',max.dist = 10)
plot(sample_vario.dist.trend2, 
     main = "Empirical Variogram with Trend 2nd",
     pch=19)


## Models fitting

# Cte Model fitting using Variogram Approach with exponential covariance
vari.cte.exp <- variofit(sample_vario.dist.cte,cov.model = "exponential", 
                         nugget = 0.2,
                         ini.cov.pars = c(60, 5),fix.nugget = TRUE)  
#vari.cte.exp

# Cte Model fitting using Variogram Approach with Matern 3/2 covariance 
vari.cte.Matern32 <- variofit(sample_vario.dist.cte,cov.model = "matern",
                          nugget = 0.2,kappa = 3/2,fix.nugget = TRUE,
                          ini.cov.pars = c(60, 5))  
#vari.cte.Matern32

# Cte Model fitting using Variogram Approach with Matern 5/2 covariance 
vari.cte.Matern52 <- variofit(sample_vario.dist.cte,cov.model = "matern",
                          nugget = 0.2,fix.nugget = TRUE,kappa = 5/2,
                          ini.cov.pars = c(60, 5))  # (partial sill, range))
#vari.cte.Matern52
```

```{r,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE,tab.cap='Estimated Parameters for Constant Trend Models',tbl-table1}
library(gt)


# Create parameter table from model outputs
params_cte <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Exponential", "Matern 3/2", "Matern 5/2"),
  Nugget = c(vari.cte.exp$nugget,
             vari.cte.Matern32$nugget,
             vari.cte.Matern52$nugget),
  Partial_Sill = c(vari.cte.exp$cov.pars[1],
                   vari.cte.Matern32$cov.pars[1],
                   vari.cte.Matern52$cov.pars[1]),
  Range = c(vari.cte.exp$cov.pars[2],
            vari.cte.Matern32$cov.pars[2],
            vari.cte.Matern52$cov.pars[2]),
  Kappa = c('-', 1.5, 2.5)
)

# Generate gt table
gt_table_cte <- params_cte %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Estimated Parameters for Constant Trend Models"
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(Nugget, Partial_Sill, Range, Kappa),
    decimals = 2
  )

gt_table_cte

```

```{r,warning=FALSE,message=FALSE,cache=TRUE,fig.cap='Cte Models Trend: Exponential vs Matern',fig-plot3}

# Visual comparison
# Base plot with empirical variogram
plot(sample_vario.dist.cte, 
     main = "Constant Trend: Exponential vs Matern", 
     pch = 19)

# Add lines for models
lines(vari.cte.exp, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
lines(vari.cte.Matern32, col = "green", lwd = 2)
lines(vari.cte.Matern52, col = "red", lwd = 2)

# Add legend
legend("bottomright", legend = c("Exponential", "Matern32", "Matern52"),
       col = c("blue", "green", "red"), lwd = 2, bty = "n")


```

## Comments

The plot (@fig-plot3) shows a comparison between empirical semi-variances (black dots) and three fitted theoretical variogram models: Exponential (blue), Matern 3/2 (green), and Matern 5/2 (red). All models capture the general increasing trend of semi-variance with distance, particularly in the mid-range distances (between lags of approximately 2 to 6) and converge near the sill, indicating a good fit overall. The Matern models, particularly Matern 5/2, fit the empirical points more closely at shorter distances, suggesting they better capture short-range spatial dependence. The Exponential model slightly overestimates semi-variance at low distances but performs comparably at longer ranges. Overall, the Matern 5/2 provides the smoothest and most accurate representation of the spatial structure.

#### Models Validation

```{r,warning=FALSE,message=FALSE,cache=TRUE,fig.cap='Cte Model Trend Validation: Exponential',fig-plot4}

library(geoR)
# Model Validation
# Set layout
par(mfrow = c(3, 2), mar = c(4, 2, 0.5, 2))

# First model
xv.ml.cte.exp <- xvalid(sst_geo,model = vari.cte.exp)
plot(xv.ml.cte.exp, error = TRUE, std.error = FALSE, pch = 19)
mtext("Exponential, Trend = cte", side = 3, line = -2,
      outer = TRUE, cex = 0.9)

```

## Comments

The diagnostic plots (@fig-plot4) provides each a set of plots that includes a scatter plot (data vs. predicted), a Q-Q plot (observed vs theoretical prob), a spatial plot (Coord X vs Coord Y), a histogram (data - predicted), and two residual plots (residuals vs predicted and residuals vs data). These plots help assess the models’ performance in terms of prediction accuracy, residual distribution, spatial patterns, and error variability.

The scatter plot shows a large spread around the diagonal line, particularly at higher predicted values (15-20), indicating substantial prediction errors. The points are more scattered, suggesting that the model with a constant trend has poor fit. The Q-Q plot exhibits a pronounced S-shape with significant deviations from the diagonal line at both tails, indicating that residuals are not normally distributed and have heavy tails. This suggests the model struggles with extreme values, leading to larger errors. The spatial plot shows a pronounced clustering of larger residuals around Coord X = 146 and Coord Y = 36-38, with more extreme residuals (larger red X’s). This indicates that the model captures spatial dependencies poorly, leaving significant not modelled spatial structure. The histogram of residuals is symmetric around zero but has a wide spread (ranging from -4 to 4) with heavy tails, reflecting larger errors and confirming the model’s difficulty with extreme values. Both Residual Plots (residuals vs predicted and residuals vs data) show no systematic bias, with residuals scattered around y = 0, but the spread is large, with numerous outliers around predicted values of 10 and 18, and data values of 5 and 20, indicating high variability in errors and a poor fit.

This model performs worse, with the largest prediction errors (scatter plot), non-normal residuals with heavy tails (Q-Q plot), pronounced spatial clustering (spatial plot), and high error variability (residual plots).

```{r,warning=FALSE,message=FALSE,cache=TRUE,fig.cap='Cte Model Trend Validation: Matern32',fig-plot5}
library(geoR)
# Model Validation
# Second model
# Set layout
par(mfrow = c(3, 2), mar = c(4, 2, 0.5, 2))
xv.ml_cte.Matern32 <- xvalid(sst_geo,model = vari.cte.Matern32)
plot(xv.ml_cte.Matern32, error = TRUE, std.error = FALSE, pch = 19)
mtext("Matern32, Trend = cte", side = 3, line = -2,
      outer = TRUE, cex = 0.9)
```

## Comments

The scatter plot from the diagnostic plots (@fig-plot5) shows the tightest clustering around the diagonal line among the three models, particularly at higher values (15-20), indicating the most accurate predictions and the best overall fit. The Q-Q plot shows residuals that are approximately normally distributed, with minor deviations at the tails, suggesting that Matern32 handles extreme values better than the other two models. The spatial plot shows clustering of larger residuals around Coord X = 146 and Coord Y = 36-38, but the pattern is the least pronounced among the three models, with fewer extreme residuals (smaller red X’s), indicating that Matern32 captures spatial dependencies more effectively. The histogram is symmetric around zero with a spread ranging from -4 to 4, tighter than Exponential and Matern52, with the least heavy tails, reflecting smaller errors overall. The residual plots show no systematic bias, with residuals scattered around y = 0, and the smallest spread among the three models, with the fewest outliers around predicted values of 10 and 18, and data values of 5 and 20, indicating the lowest error variability.

In summary, Matern32 performs the best, with the tightest scatter plot clustering, a Q-Q plot showing the smallest deviations (residuals approximately normal with minor tail deviations), and the least spatial clustering, suggesting the most effective capture of spatial dependencies. Its histogram and residual plots show the smallest spread and fewest outliers, confirming the lowest error variability, likely due to its smoother kernel ($\nu$ = 3/2) better modelling spatial correlation compared to Matern52 $\nu$ = 5/2) and Exponential $\nu$ = 1/2).

```{r,warning=FALSE,message=FALSE,fig.cap='Cte Model Trend Validation: Matern52',fig-plot6}
# Model Validation
library(geoR)
# Third model
# Set layout
par(mfrow = c(3, 2), mar = c(4, 2, 0.5, 2))
xv.ml_cte.Matern52 <- xvalid(sst_geo,model = vari.cte.Matern52)
plot(xv.ml_cte.Matern52, error = TRUE, std.error = FALSE, pch = 19)
mtext("Matern52, Trend cte", side = 3, line = -2, 
      outer = TRUE, cex = 0.9)
```

## Comments

The scatter plot shows a tighter clustering around the diagonal line compared to the Exponential model, particularly at mid-range predicted values (10-15), but the spread is still noticeable at higher values (15-20). This indicates a better fit than Exponential but not as good as Matern32 (@fig-plot6). The Q-Q plot shows moderate deviations from the diagonal line at the tails, less severe than Matern52 but more than Exponential, suggesting that residuals are not perfectly normally distributed and the model struggles with extreme values to a lesser extent. The spatial plot shows clustering of larger residuals around Coord X = 146 and Coord Y = 36-38, similar to Exponential, but the intensity is less pronounced (fewer extreme residuals), indicating that Matern52 captures some spatial dependencies better than Exponential. The histogram is symmetric around zero with a spread ranging from -4 to 4, slightly tighter than Exponential, reflecting moderate errors. The residual plots show no systematic bias, with residuals scattered around y = 0, and the spread is smaller than Exponential, with fewer outliers around predicted values of 10 and 18, and data values of 5 and 20, indicating reduced error variability compared to Exponential. Overall, Matern52 performs better, with a tighter scatter plot, a Q-Q plot showing moderate deviations (less severe than Exponential), and reduced spatial clustering, though still noticeable around the same coordinates, indicating improved but imperfect spatial modelling. Its residuals have a slightly tighter spread in the histogram and fewer outliers in the residual plots.

In conclusion, the Exponential model performs the worst, with the largest prediction errors (scatter plot), non-normal residuals with heavy tails (Q-Q plot), pronounced spatial clustering (spatial plot), and high error variability (residual plots). The Matern52 one fits better than Exponential, with a tighter fit, more normal residuals, less spatial clustering, and reduced error variability, but it still underperforms compared to Matern32. Matern32 model performs the best, with the tightest fit, most normal residuals, least spatial clustering, and lowest error variability, indicating that its smoother kernel ($\nu$ = 3/2) captures spatial dependencies more effectively than Exponential ($\nu$ = 1/2) and Matern52 ($\nu$ = 5/2).

## Comments

The plot (@fig-plot7) shows that the empirical semi-variance values are relatively constant, fluctuating around a value of 4 across distances from 0 to 12, with a slight dip near distance 0. It compares Exponential, Matern32, and Matern52 models against the empirical semivariogram. The inclusion of a linear trend flattens the variogram, indicating that much of the large-scale spatial variation has been removed. While the Matern models quickly reach a sill, suggesting very short-range dependence, the Exponential model provides a smoother rise that better matches the empirical pattern. Overall, the Exponential model offers a more appropriate fit after detrending, capturing the remaining spatial structure more effectively.

Overall, the Matern52 with constant trend seems to be the best overall model, as it offers a more flexible and accurate representation of spatial structure without assuming a linear trend. However, if a linear spatial trend is theoretically justified or strongly supported by exploratory analysis, the Exponential with first-order trend is a good alternative that captures the residual spatial variability adequately.

#### Models Validation

## Comments

The diagnostic plots (@fig-plot8, @fig-plot9, @fig-plot10) reveal that the Exponential model's scatter plot shows the tightest alignment between predicted and observed data, indicating strong predictive accuracy, but its Q-Q plot exhibits a wider deviation from the theoretical distribution, particularly at the tails, suggesting issues with capturing extreme values, and its residuals histogram shows some skewness, indicating potential bias. In contrast, the Matern32 and Matern52 models have scatter plots with wider spreads, reflecting less precise predictions, but their Q-Q plots deviate only slightly from the theoretical distribution, suggesting a better fit for extreme values. Matern32's residuals histogram is the most symmetric around zero, indicating minimal bias and the best overall performance, while Matern52's histogram shows slightly more skewness but less than the Exponential, placing its performance between the two. Therefore, despite the Exponential's tighter scatter plot, Matern32 performs the best due to its minimal Q-Q deviation and balanced residuals, followed by Matern52, with the Exponential performing the poorest due to its wider Q-Q deviation and bias. In summary, compared to Matern32 constant trend, the Matern32 first order trend performs the best overall.

#### Kriging Approach Model for the best model Matern32 with first order trend

```{r,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE,cache=TRUE,fig.cap='1st Models Trend: Matern32',fig-plot11,fig.show="asis"}
# Create a prediction grid
# Get bounding box from your sample coordinates
x.range <- range(sst_geo$coords[, 1])  # Longitude
y.range <- range(sst_geo$coords[, 2])  # Latitude

# Generate a 100x100 prediction grid
grid <- expand.grid(
  lon = seq(x.range[1], x.range[2], length.out = 100),
  lat = seq(y.range[1], y.range[2], length.out = 100)
)

# Kriging on the grid using Matern32 model
kriged_grid_trend1.Matern32 <- krige.conv(sst_geo,
                              locations = as.matrix(grid),
                              krige = krige.control(trend.d = "1st",
                              obj.model = vari.trend1.Matern32))


# 1. Kriging Mean
image(kriged_grid_trend1.Matern32,
      col = viridis::viridis(100),
      zlim = c(0, max(kriged_grid_trend1.Matern32$predict, na.rm = TRUE)),
      coords.data = sst_geo$coords,
      main = 'Kriging Mean',
      xlab = 'Longitude', ylab = 'Latitude')
```

```{r,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE,cache=TRUE,fig.cap='1st Models Trend: Matern32',fig-plot12,fig.show="asis"}

# 2. Kriging Variance
```

## Comments

The Kriging Mean and Kriging Variance plots (@fig-plot11, @fig-plot12) illustrate the predictive performance of a kriging model over a spatial region defined by longitude (135 to 155) and latitude (32 to 40), with data points scattered across the area. The Kriging Mean plot shows a smooth gradient from yellow (lower values, \~5) in the southwest to blue (higher values, \~20) in the northeast, indicating a clear spatial trend where the predicted values increase diagonally from the bottom-left to the top-right, aligning with the data points' distribution. In contrast, the Kriging Variance plot is uniformly red, suggesting a constant predictive variance (around 2-3) across the entire region, which implies the model assumes consistent uncertainty regardless of location. This uniformity in variance might indicate that the kriging model, while capturing the mean trend effectively, does not account for spatial variations in uncertainty, potentially due to the sparse data or a simplistic covariance structure, limiting its ability to reflect localised prediction reliability.

```{r,tab.cap='Gaussian Process Model Comparison',tbl-table3}
  ) %>%

    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = "Beta")
  )

```

## Comments

This table (@tbl-table3) presents maximum likelihood estimates for Gaussian Process (GP) models with a constant mean, using Exponential and Matérn covariance functions ($\nu$ = 3/2 and 5/2). The Exponential model performs best, with the lowest AIC (302.416) and highest log-likelihood (−148.208), indicating a strong overall fit. It also has the largest range (7.259) and highest partial sill (28.418), suggesting it captures broader and stronger spatial dependence compared to the Matérn models. Both Matérn models yield shorter range parameters and higher AIC values, implying less effective modelling of the spatial structure under a constant mean assumption.

## Comments

The diagnostic plots (@fig-plot13, @fig-plot14, @fig-plot15) for the Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) models evaluate three Gaussian Process models, Exponential, Matérn ($\nu$=3/2), and Matérn ($\nu$=5/2), all with a constant trend. For the Exponential model, the scatter plot shows a tight linear trend between observed and predicted data, the Q-Q plot aligns closely with the theoretical line with minimal tail deviation, the spatial plot indicates high accuracy with close matches between observed and predicted points, the residual histogram is centered around zero with most residuals between -1 and 1, and residual scatter plots confirm homoscedasticity with no bias and low spread. The Matérn ($\nu$=5/2) model’s scatter plot shows a slightly looser linear trend, the Q-Q plot has noticeable tail deviations, the spatial plot shows moderate alignment, the residual histogram spans -2 to 2, and residual plots indicate homoscedasticity but greater uncertainty. The Matérn ($\nu$=3/2) model, with an AIC (324.887) between Exponential (302.416) and Matérn ($\nu$=5/2) (335.133), likely shows intermediate performance, with slightly better alignment and residuals than Matérn ($\nu$=5/2) but not as tight as Exponential. Overall, the Exponential model is the best, as its superior fit, distribution capture, and smaller residuals align with its lowest AIC, making it the optimal choice for this dataset.

## Comments

The table ( @tbl-table4) compares first-order trend Gaussian Process (GP) models estimated via maximum likelihood, using three different covariance functions: Exponential, Matérn $\nu$ = 3/2, and Matérn $\nu$ = 5/2. All models include spatial trend terms for longitude and latitude, and the nugget ($\tau^2$) is fixed at 1.5 across all cases. The Matérn models outperform the Exponential model in terms of both log-likelihood and AIC, indicating a better fit to the data. Among them, the Matérn $\nu$ = 5/2 model achieves the lowest AIC (341.191) and a higher log-likelihood (−165.595) than the Exponential model, suggesting it captures the spatial structure more effectively. Additionally, the Matérn models have shorter range parameters, implying they model finer-scale spatial dependence. The Matérn $\nu$ = 5/2 model with a first-order trend provides the best fit among the models considered, offering both improved likelihood and AIC while accounting for local spatial variation through a flexible covariance structure.

In comparison to the first-order trend models, all constant mean models show better fit statistics, particularly the Exponential model, which substantially outperforms all first-order trend variants. This indicates that incorporating spatial trends via longitude and latitude does not improve model performance likely because the spatial variation is better captured through the covariance structure alone rather than explicit trends.

In conclusion, the Exponential GP model with a constant mean remains the best overall model, offering the most efficient balance of model complexity and spatial explanatory power. Adding a trend increases model complexity without improving fit, as reflected by higher AIC values in the trend-based models.

## Comments

The diagnostic plots (@fig-plot16, @fig-plot17, @fig-plot18) for the Matérn ($\nu$=3/2) model with a first-order trend show a strong linear trend in the scatter plot of observed vs. predicted data with some scatter, a Q-Q plot with slight tail deviations indicating issues with extreme values, a spatial plot with moderate alignment between observed and predicted points, a residual histogram centered around zero with most residuals between -2 and 2, and residual scatter plots confirming homoscedasticity but reflecting some predictive uncertainty. The Matérn ($\nu$=5/2) first-order trend model (AIC: 341.191) performs similarly but slightly better, with a tighter Q-Q plot alignment, while the Exponential first-order trend model (AIC: 345.286) shows the weakest fit. Compared to the constant trend (CTE) models, where the Exponential model excelled (AIC: 302.416) with tighter scatter, better Q-Q alignment, more accurate spatial predictions, and residuals mostly between -1 and 1, followed by Matérn ($\nu$=3/2) (AIC: 324.887) and Matérn ($\nu$=5/2) (AIC: 335.133), the CTE models consistently outperform their first-order trend counterparts, as their lower AICs and better diagnostic metrics indicate a superior balance of fit and simplicity, making the CTE Exponential model the best overall choice for this dataset.

```{r,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE,tab.cap='Geostatistical Model Comparison using MLE',tbl-table5}
    rows = 1:3
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "gray95"),
    locations = cells_row_groups()
  ) %>%
  tab_options(
    table.width = "100%",  # Keep table width at 100%
    table.font.size = "12px",  # Reduce font size to fit more content
    column_labels.font.size = "10px",  # Smaller font for column headers
    row_group.font.size = "12px",
    row_group.font.weight = "bold",
    table.align = "center"
  ) %>%
  cols_width(
    Model ~ px(100),  # Manually set column widths to ensure fit
    Intercept ~ px(80),
    Lon_Coeff ~ px(60),
    Lat_Coeff ~ px(60),
    Nugget ~ px(60),
    Partial_Sill ~ px(60),
    Range ~ px(60),
    LogLik ~ px(60),
    AIC ~ px(60)
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(align = "center", v_align = "middle"),
    locations = cells_body()
  ) %>%
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = "Nugget fixed at 1.5 for 1st trend and 0.2 for cte trend",
    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = "Nugget")
  ) %>%
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = "Comparison of spatial covariance structures with different mean specifications"
  )
```

## Comments

The comparison table (@tbl-table5) summarises geostatistical models fitted using maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), contrasting constant mean models with first-order trend models across three covariance structures: Exponential, Matérn $\nu$ = 3/2, and Matérn $\nu$ = 5/2. Among the constant mean models, the Exponential covariance model achieves the lowest AIC (302.416) and highest log-likelihood (−148.208), indicating the best fit in that group. For the first-order trend models, all three exhibit higher AIC values and lower log-likelihoods, suggesting poorer overall fit despite accounting for spatial trends via longitude and latitude.

Interestingly, while the trend models reduce the sill and range substantially, indicating less residual spatial dependence after removing the large-scale trend their performance metrics (AIC and log-likelihood) do not improve. This implies that introducing a linear spatial trend does not enhance the explanatory power of the model in this case.

In conclusion, the Exponential model with a constant mean provides the best overall fit to the data, balancing model simplicity and spatial explanatory power as indicated by the lowest AIC and best likelihood score.

## Comments

The Gaussian Process (GP) predictive mean and variance plots (@fig-plot19, @fig-plot20) are based on a Sea Surface Temperature (SST) dataset, mapping SST values across a spatial region defined by longitude (135 to 155) and latitude (32 to 40), with observed SST data points shown as black dots. The predictive mean plot displays a heatmap where colours indicate SST values, transitioning from lower temperatures (yellow, around 32 latitude and 135-140 longitude) to higher temperatures (blue, around 38 latitude and 150-155 longitude), revealing a clear southwest-to-northeast warming trend, consistent with a first-order trend model for SST. The predictive variance plot, using the same grid, shows variance levels with colours from yellow (low variance) to red (high variance), with low variance in data-dense areas (e.g., around 34 latitude and 140-145 longitude), indicating high confidence in SST predictions, and high variance in the northeast (around 38 latitude and 150-155 longitude) where data is sparse, reflecting greater uncertainty in SST estimates. These plots suggest the GP model effectively captures the spatial trend in SST but has higher predictive reliability in regions with more SST observations and less certainty in sparsely sampled areas.

### Bayesian Models fitting

```{r,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE,results='hide'}
## Bayesian Models fitting
library(geoR)
# Coarser prediction grid (30x30 = 900 points)
# Create prediction grid
x.range <- range(sst_geo$coords[, 1])  # Longitude
y.range <- range(sst_geo$coords[, 2])  # Latitude
pred_grid <- as.matrix(expand.grid(
  lon = seq(x.range[1], x.range[2], length.out = 30),
  lat = seq(y.range[1], y.range[2], length.out = 30)
))


# Constant Mean (Exponential Covariance)
bayes_cte_exp <- krige.bayes(
  geodata = sst_geo,
  locations = pred_grid,
  model = model.control(
    trend.d = "cte",
    trend.l = "cte",
    cov.model = "exponential"
  ),
  prior = prior.control(
    beta.prior = "flat",
    sigmasq.prior = "uniform",
    sigmasq = c(1, 30),
    phi.prior = "reciprocal",
    phi.discrete = seq(0.5, 10, length.out = 51),
    tausq.rel.prior = "uniform",
    tausq.rel.discrete = seq(0.05, 0.15, length.out = 11)
  ),
  output = output.control(moments = TRUE, signal = TRUE,
                          n.predictive = 1000)
)

```

```{r,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE,cache=TRUE,tab.cap='Bayesian Kriging Parameters',tbl-table7}
library(geoR)
library(gt)

# Extract posterior means for parameters
param_table <- data.frame(
  Parameter = c("Intercept(beta0)", 
                "Partial Sill(sigmasq)", 
                "Range(phi)", 
                "Nugget(tausq)"),
  Mean = c(
    mean(bayes_cte_exp$posterior$sample$beta),
    mean(bayes_cte_exp$posterior$sample$sigmasq),
    mean(bayes_cte_exp$posterior$sample$phi),
    mean(bayes_cte_exp$posterior$sample$tausq.rel) * 
      mean(bayes_cte_exp$posterior$sample$sigmasq)
  ),
  SD = c(
    sd(bayes_cte_exp$posterior$sample$beta),
    sd(bayes_cte_exp$posterior$sample$sigmasq),
    sd(bayes_cte_exp$posterior$sample$phi),
    sd(bayes_cte_exp$posterior$sample$tausq.rel * 
         bayes_cte_exp$posterior$sample$sigmasq)
  )
)

# Create minimal gt table
param_table %>% 
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(decimals = 3) %>%
  cols_label(
    Parameter = "Parameter",
    Mean = "Posterior Mean", 
    SD = "Std. Dev."
  ) %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Bayesian Kriging Parameters",
    subtitle = "Constant Mean with Exponential Covariance"
  ) %>%
  tab_options(
    table.width = pct(60),
    column_labels.font.weight = "bold"
  ) %>%
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = "Nugget calculated as tausq = tausq.rel × sigmasq",
    locations = cells_body(columns = Parameter, rows = 4)
  )
```

## Comments

The table (@tbl-table7) presents Bayesian posterior mean estimates model with a constant mean and exponential covariance structure yielded the following parameter estimates. The intercept ( $\beta_0$ = 15.222 ± 1.451) represents the baseline sea surface temperature across the study area. The spatial dependence structure shows a partial sill ( $\sigma^2$ = 9.209 ± 1.830), indicating substantial spatial variation in SST, with an effective range ( $\phi$ = 3.093 ± 0.894) suggesting correlations persist over moderate distances. The nugget effect ( $\tau^2$ = 0.476 ± 0.099) accounts for measurement error and micro-scale variation, representing about 5% of the total variation (nugget/total sill ratio). The relatively small standard deviations compared to the mean estimates suggest precise parameter estimation. This exponential covariance model suggests smoothly varying SST patterns with moderate spatial continuity across the study region.

```{r,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE,tab.cap='Model Comparison: ML vs Bayesian Approaches',tbl-table8}

library(gt)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

# Extract posterior means from Bayesian models
extract_bayes_means <- function(model) {
  if ("sample" %in% names(model$posterior)) {
    samples <- model$posterior$sample
    list(
      `Intercept(beta0)` = if ("beta" %in% names(samples)) mean(samples$beta) else 
                        if ("beta0" %in% names(samples)) mean(samples$beta0) else NA_real_,
      `Sill` = mean(samples$sigmasq),
      `Range` = mean(samples$phi),
      `Nugget` = mean(samples$tausq.rel) * mean(samples$sigmasq)
    )
  } else {
    list(
      `Intercept(beta0)` = NA_real_,
      `Sill` = NA_real_, `Range` = NA_real_, `Nugget` = NA_real_
    )
  }
}

# Extract means from both models
cte_means <- extract_bayes_means(bayes_cte_exp)
#trend_means <- extract_bayes_means(bayes_1st_mat32)

# Create comparison data frame with proper parameter names
param_names <- c("Intercept (beta0)", "Nugget(tausq)", 
                 "Sill(sigmasq)", "Range(phi)")

comparison_df <- data.frame(
  Parameter = factor(param_names, levels = param_names),
  ML_Constant = c(14.703, 0.200, 28.418, 7.259),
  Bayes_Constant = c(
    cte_means$`Intercept(beta0)`,
    cte_means$`Nugget`, cte_means$`Sill`, cte_means$`Range`
  )
)

# Create and format the gt table
gt_table <- comparison_df %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -Parameter,
    names_to = c("Method", "Model"),
    names_sep = "_",
    values_to = "Value"
  ) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = "Method",
    values_from = "Value"
  ) %>%
  arrange(Model, Parameter) %>%
  gt(groupname_col = "Model") %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c("ML", "Bayes"),
    decimals = 3
  ) %>%
  sub_missing(
    columns = everything(),
    missing_text = "—"
  ) %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Model Comparison: ML vs Bayesian Approaches",
    subtitle = "Parameter Estimates with Mathematical Notation"
  ) %>%
  cols_label(
    Parameter = "Parameter",
    ML = "Maximum Likelihood",
    Bayes = "Bayesian Posterior Mean"
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(style = "italic"),
    locations = cells_row_groups()
  ) %>%
  tab_options(
    table.width = "100%",
    column_labels.font.size = 14,
    table.font.size = 12,
    column_labels.padding = px(10)
  ) %>%
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = "Nugget calculated as tausq = tausq.rel × sigmasq",
    locations = cells_body(columns = "Bayes", rows = Parameter == "Nugget")
  ) %>%
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = "Source: Sea Surface Temperature (SST) dataset \n in the
 Kuroshio current off Japan from the \n first two days of January 1996"
  )

# Display the table
gt_table
```

## Comments

The table ( @tbl-table8) compares parameter estimates between the Maximum Likelihood (ML) and Bayesian approaches under a constant mean Gaussian Process model. The Bayesian posterior mean for the intercept ($\beta_0$ = 15.222) is slightly higher than the ML estimate (14.703), indicating a similar central tendency. However, the Bayesian approach estimates a much larger nugget ( $\tau^2$= 0.476 vs. 0.200), suggesting it captures more measurement noise or microscale variation. In contrast, the Bayesian sill ($\sigma^2$ = 9.209) and range ($phi$ = 3.093) are notably smaller than their ML counterparts (28.418 and 7.259), implying the Bayesian model attributes less variation to spatial structure and assumes a shorter spatial correlation length. Overall, the Bayesian model results in a smoother, more locally dependent spatial process with greater uncertainty at small scales. Based on the parameter estimates, the Maximum Likelihood (ML) model attributes more variation to spatial structure (higher sill and longer range), while the Bayesian model accounts for greater measurement error (higher nugget) and assumes a shorter spatial correlation range. Although both models estimate similar intercepts, the ML model suggests a stronger and more extensive spatial dependence. However, the Bayesian approach offers a more conservative, locally adaptive view of spatial variation by balancing nugget and sill more distinctly.

## Comments

The Bayesian approach prediction plots ( @fig-plot21) for the Exponential model with a constant trend (Cte trend) applied to the Sea Surface Temperature (SST) dataset reveal key insights across a spatial region defined by longitude (140 to 150) and latitude (30 to 38). The predictive mean plot shows a uniform yellow colour, indicating a constant SST mean across the region, consistent with the Cte trend assumption, with observed data points (yellow squares) sparsely distributed, suggesting limited data coverage. The predictive variance plot displays a heatmap with high variance (red) across most of the region, indicating significant uncertainty in SST predictions, particularly where data points are absent, as the model lacks sufficient observations to reduce uncertainty. Two simulation plots (Simulation 1 and Simulation 2) present possible SST realisations, showing sparse yellow-green points that vary slightly in placement but align with the observed data locations, reflecting the model’s attempt to simulate SST values under the constant trend assumption. Overall, the Bayesian approach highlights a uniform SST mean prediction with high uncertainty due to sparse data, and the simulations provide plausible SST scenarios consistent with the limited observations.

```{r,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE,fig.cap='Bayesian Posterior distribution',fig-plot22}

par(mfrow = c(2, 2),mar=c(4,4,2,4),oma=c(0,0,2,0))  # Set up 2x2 plot grid

# 1. Range (ϕ) posterior
if(!is.null(bayes_cte_exp$posterior$sample$phi)) {
  hist(bayes_cte_exp$posterior$sample$phi, 
       main = "Posterior: Range (ϕ)",
       xlab = "Range", col = "lightblue", freq = FALSE)
  lines(density(bayes_cte_exp$posterior$sample$phi), 
        col = "blue", lwd = 2)
}

# 2. Sill (σ²) posterior
if(!is.null(bayes_cte_exp$posterior$sample$sigmasq)) {
  hist(bayes_cte_exp$posterior$sample$sigmasq, 
       main = "Posterior: Sill (σ²)",
       xlab = "Partial Sill", col = "lightgreen", freq = FALSE)
  lines(density(bayes_cte_exp$posterior$sample$sigmasq), 
        col = "darkgreen", lwd = 2)
}

# 3. Nugget (τ²) posterior
if(!is.null(bayes_cte_exp$posterior$sample$tausq.rel)) {
  nugget <- bayes_cte_exp$posterior$sample$tausq.rel * 
            mean(bayes_cte_exp$posterior$sample$sigmasq)
  hist(nugget,
       main = "Posterior: Nugget (τ²)",
       xlab = "Nugget", col = "pink", freq = FALSE)
  lines(density(nugget), 
        col = "red", lwd = 2)
}

# 4. Intercept (β₀) posterior
if(!is.null(bayes_cte_exp$posterior$sample$beta)) {
  hist(bayes_cte_exp$posterior$sample$beta,
       main = "Posterior: Intercept (beta) ",
       xlab = "Intercept", col = "lightyellow", freq = FALSE)
  lines(density(bayes_cte_exp$posterior$sample$beta), 
        col = "orange", lwd = 2)
}
```

## Comments

The plots (@fig-plot22) display the posterior distributions of four parameters Range (phi), Partial Sill (sigmasq), Nugget (tausq), and Intercept (beta) from a Bayesian kriging model with a constant trend. The posterior for phi (Range) peaks around 2 to 4, indicating the spatial range of correlation is relatively short, with a density dropping sharply beyond 6, suggesting the model is confident in a smaller range. The Partial Sill (sigmasq) posterior centers around 10 to 12, with a spread from 6 to 18, reflecting moderate uncertainty in the variance of the spatial process, but a clear preference for values around 10. The Nugget (tausq) posterior is heavily skewed, peaking sharply near 0.5 and dropping quickly, with most density below 0.7, indicating a small nugget effect and suggesting low measurement error or micro-scale variability. Finally, the Intercept (beta) posterior is centered around 16, with a range from 10 to 20, showing a normal-like distribution and moderate uncertainty in the mean level of the process. Overall, the model provides well-defined estimates for these parameters, with the Nugget being the most constrained and the Intercept showing the widest uncertainty.

## Comments

The Kriging Prediction Results for the 5 locations plot (@fig-plot23, @fig-plot24) shows the predictive mean and variance using a standard kriging model. The mean plot displays a smooth gradient from yellow (lower values) to purple (higher values, around 20), with higher predictions in the northwest (Latitude \~38, Longitude \~140), decreasing towards the southeast. The variance plot, uniformly orange, indicates a constant predictive variance across the region, suggesting the model assumes consistent uncertainty (around 2-3) regardless of location, which might reflect limited data (5 points) or a simplistic model structure, potentially underestimating spatial variability in uncertainty.

The Gaussian Process prediction plots (@fig-plot25, @fig-plot26) also show predictive mean and variance but with a different approach. The mean plot mirrors the kriging pattern, with higher values (purple, \~20) in the northwest and lower values (yellow, \~5) in the southeast, aligning with the data points. However, the variance plot reveals more spatial structure, with higher uncertainty (red, \~5) near the data points (e.g., Latitude 32-34, Longitude 144-148) and lower variance (yellow, \~1) in areas farther away, indicating the Gaussian Process model better captures spatial variation in uncertainty, leveraging its flexible covariance structure.

The Bayesian Predictive plots (@fig-plot27) using an Exponential covariance with constant trend show similar trends in the mean, with higher predictions in the northwest (purple, \~20) and lower in the southeast (yellow, \~5), consistent with the other models. The variance plot, however, shows significant spatial variation, with high uncertainty (red, \~5) near data points and lower uncertainty (yellow, \~1) in interpolated areas, similar to the Gaussian Process but with slightly more pronounced contrasts, reflecting the Bayesian model's ability to incorporate prior uncertainty and adapt to sparse data.

The Simulation 1 plot (Exp, Cte trend) represents a simulated predictive mean using an Exponential covariance model with a constant trend. The plot shows a pixelated pattern with values ranging from blue (\~5) to yellow (\~20), but the distribution appears less smooth, with abrupt transitions and scattered high/low values, suggesting the simulation struggles to capture the underlying spatial trend accurately, likely due to overfitting to the sparse 5-point data or poor parameter estimation. While the Simulation 2 (Exp, Cte trend) plot, another simulation with the same model, also shows a pixelated pattern but with a slightly different distribution of values. It ranges from blue (\~5) to yellow (\~20), with clusters of high and low predictions that don't align smoothly with the spatial gradient seen in the other models, indicating inconsistent predictions and potential issues with the simulation's ability to generalise from limited data.

Comparing the models, the Kriging model provides a smooth mean prediction but fails to capture spatial variation in uncertainty, making it less reliable for sparse data. The Gaussian Process and Bayesian models both excel in capturing spatial trends in both mean and variance, with the Bayesian model showing slightly more defined variance patterns, likely due to its incorporation of prior distributions. The simulation models (Simulation 1 and 2) perform poorly, producing inconsistent and pixelated predictions that fail to reflect the underlying spatial structure. In terms of prediction, the Bayesian model is the best, as it balances accurate mean predictions with spatially adaptive variance, effectively handling the uncertainty inherent in the sparse 5-point dataset.

# Question 2: Atlantic Overturning Circulation

## (a) Plot the data and comment on any patterns/trends observed

```{r}
# load the dataset
amoc <- load("D:/Bureau/University of Exeter UK/Modules/Data Science and Statistical Modelling in Space and Time/Coursework/MOC.Rdata")

#head(MOCmean)


```

```{r,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE,fig.cap='AMOC Strength plot Jan 2017-Feb 2023',fig-plot28}
# Load required packages
library(ggfortify)
library(ggplot2)
library(zoo)

# Create the time series
moc.ts <- ts(MOCmean, start = c(2017, 1),end = c(2023,2), frequency = 12)

# Convert to zoo with Date index
time_dates <- as.Date(as.yearmon(time(moc.ts)))
moc.zoo <- zoo(coredata(moc.ts), order.by = time_dates)

# Plot with autoplot and scale_x_date
p <- autoplot(moc.zoo, ts.color = "blue", ts.size = 1) +
  labs(title = "Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) \n Jan 2017-Feb 2023",
       y = "Strength Circulation",
       x = "Year") +
  scale_x_date(
    breaks = "1 year",  # Major breaks every year
    minor_breaks = "3 months",  # Minor breaks every 3 months
    limits = as.Date(c("2017-01-01", "2023-02-01")),  # Jan 2017 to Feb 2023
    date_labels = "%Y",  # Label as years
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "gray", linetype = "dotted"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_line(color = "gray", linetype = "dotted")
  )

# Display the plot
print(p)
```

### Comments

The plot of AMOC strength at 26°N from January 2017 to February 2023 shows a relatively stable mean strength of around 15–16 , with no clear long-term trend of strengthening or weakening over this period (@fig-plot28). A pronounced seasonal cycle is evident, with annual peaks reaching up to 20–24 (likely in winter months, e.g., December–February) and troughs dipping to 8–12 (likely in summer months, e.g., June–August), reflecting seasonal variations in atmospheric or oceanic forcing. The series exhibits significant month-to-month variability, with fluctuations of 5–10 within a year, and notable anomalies, such as a sharp dip below 10 in mid-2020 followed by a recovery to above 20, possibly due to an extreme climatic event. The amplitude of fluctuations varies over time, with periods like 2019 showing smaller swings and 2020–2022 showing larger ones, suggesting potential non-stationarity in variance, which should be considered in modelling and forecasting efforts

## (b) ARMA and ARIMA models fitting

```{r,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE}
# Exclusion of the Last 8 Months

# Exclude the last 8 months (Jul 2022 to Feb 2023)
moc.ts.train <- window(moc.ts, start = c(2017, 1), end = c(2022, 6))

```

### Comments

From the earlier plot (which included the full dataset), we observed that there is no clear long-term trend in the mean (it fluctuates around 15–16), a strong seasonal pattern with annual cycles and the variance appears to vary slightly over time (e.g., larger swings in 2020 compared to 2019). In order to fit the ARMA or ARIMA models without using auto.arima function, we ill plot the Autocorrelation Function (ACF) and Partial Autocorrelation Function (PACF) to determine order of the model's paramaters.

```{r,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE,tab.cap='Augmented Dickey-Fuller Test for Quarterly AMOC Strength',tbl-table9}
library(tseries)
# If the p-value < 0.05, the series is stationary 
# (reject the null hypothesis of a unit root).
# If the p-value > 0.05, the series is non-stationary, 
# and differencing may be needed (ARIMA).

adf.test(moc.ts.train)


# Load the gt library
library(gt)

# Create data frame for ADF test results
adf_data <- data.frame(
  Parameter = c("Dickey-Fuller", "Lag order", "p-value"),
  Value = c(-4.1823, 4, 0.01)
)

# Create the table with gt
adf_table <- gt(data = adf_data, rowname_col = "Parameter") %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Augmented Dickey-Fuller Test for Quarterly AMOC Strength"
  ) %>%
  cols_label(
    Value = "Value"
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = "Value",
    rows = c(1, 3),  # Dickey-Fuller and p-value
    decimals = 3
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = "Value",
    rows = 2,  # Lag order
    decimals = 0
  ) %>%
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = "Alternative Hypothesis: Stationary"
  )

# Display the table
adf_table
```

### Comments

Before proceeding to model fitting, we performed the Augmented Dickey-Fuller Test (ADF) to check the stationarity of the data. The p-value 0.01 from the Augmented Dickey-Fuller Test for Quarterly AMOC Strength is less than 0.05, so we reject the null hypothesis of a unit root (@tbl-table9). This indicates that the series is stationary without differencing. Since the series is stationary, we can then fit ARMAs model directly without differencing ($𝑑$ = 0). However, we’ll also explore ARIMA models with $𝑑$ = 1 to compare and see if differencing might still improve the fit by addressing any residual trends or variance issues.

```{r,fig.cap='ACF and PACF plots of AMOC Strength',fig-plot29}
# Autocorrelation Function (ACF) and Partial Autocorrelation Function (PACF)
par(mfrow=c(1,2),mar=c(4,4,4,4))
acf(moc.ts.train, main = "ACF of AMOC Strength")
pacf(moc.ts.train, main = "PACF of AMOC Strength")
```

### Comments

The ACF and PACF plots (@fig-plot29) of the AMOC strength data (from January 2017 to June 2022, excluding the last 8 months) provide insights into the time series structure for fitting ARMA and ARIMA models without seasonal components. The ACF plot shows a significant spike at lag 1 (around 0.3), followed by smaller, mostly insignificant spikes at higher lags, with some periodic patterns at lags around 1.0 (approximately 12 months), indicating the presence of seasonality despite the instruction to ignore seasonal components. This suggests an MA(1) component might be appropriate due to the sharp drop after lag 1 (about 0.2). The PACF plot exhibits a significant spike at lag 1 (around 0.2), suggesting a possible AR(1) component, as the PACF cuts off after lag 1. The slow decay in the ACF and the significant lags in the PACF suggest the series may be non-stationary, likely requiring differencing for an ARIMA model, while the patterns at lag 1 in both plots support testing ARMA(1,1) or ARIMA(1,1,1) models to capture the short-term dependencies in the data.

### ARMA Models

#### ARMA(1,0)

```{r,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE}
# ARMA(1,0) = AR(1)
arma10 <- arima(moc.ts.train, order = c(1, 0, 0),seasonal = c(0,0,0))
#summary(arma10)

```

```{r,tab.cap='ARMA(1,0) Model Summary',tbl-table10,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE}
library(gt)

# Create a data frame with the model summary information
arma10_summary <- data.frame(
  Parameter = c("ar1", "Intercept", "sigma^2", "AIC", "Log Likelihood"),
  Value = c(arma10$coef[1], arma10$coef[2], arma10$sigma2, arma10$aic, arma10$loglik),
  Std.Error = c(sqrt(arma10$var.coef[1,1]), sqrt(arma10$var.coef[2,2]), NA, NA, NA)
)

# Create the gt table
arma10_summary %>% 
  gt() %>% 
  tab_header(
    title = "ARMA(1,0) Model Summary",
    subtitle = "Summary of the fitted ARMA(1,0) model"
  ) %>% 
  fmt_number(
    columns = c("Value", "Std.Error"),
    decimals = 3
  ) %>% 
  cols_label(
    Parameter = "Parameter",
    Value = "Estimate",
    Std.Error = "Std. Error"
  ) %>% 
  fmt_missing(
    columns = "Std.Error",  # Fixed: column name as string
    missing_text = "-"
  ) %>% 
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = "Square root of the variance of the white noise",
    locations = cells_body(columns = "Std.Error", rows = 3)
  ) %>% 
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = "Akaike Information Criterion",
    locations = cells_body(columns = "Parameter", rows = 4)
  )
```

### Comments

The summary table for the ARMA(1,0) model reveals key model characteristics (@tbl-table10). The model shows an AR(1) with coefficient (ar1) of 0.154 and a standard error of 0.121. This indicates a modest positive autocorrelation that is not statistically significant (due to the relatively large standard error), and an intercept of 16.772 (standard error 0.416), suggesting a mean AMOC strength of around 16.77, consistent with the data’s average. The model fit statistics show a $\sigma^2$ of 8.21, log likelihood of -163.14, and AIC of 332.28, providing a baseline for model comparison, though the presence of seasonality (not modelled) likely impacts these metrics.

```{r,fig.cap='Diagnostics plots',fig-plot30,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE}
# Residuals checking
par(mfrow=c(1,2),mar=c(4,4,3.5,2))
tsdiag(arma10)  
```

### Comments

The diagnostic plots (@fig-plot30) for the ARMA(1,0) model provide insights into the model’s adequacy. The "Standardized Residuals" plot shows residuals fluctuating around zero with no clear trend or pattern over time, suggesting the model captures the mean structure well, though some residuals exceed ±2, indicating potential outliers or unmodelled variability. The "ACF of Residuals" plot reveals significant spikes at lags around 0.5, 1.0, and 1.5 (approximately 6, 12, and 18 months), reflecting the unmodelled seasonal pattern (annual cycle) in the data, as the problem specified no seasonal components. This indicates that the ARMA(1,0) model fails to capture the seasonal autocorrelation. The "p-values for Ljung-Box statistic" plot shows p-values consistently below 0.05 for lags 1 to 10, rejecting the null hypothesis of no autocorrelation in the residuals, further confirming the presence of none modelled structure, likely due to seasonality. Overall, while the ARMA(1,0) model fits the mean reasonably well, its inability to account for the seasonal pattern suggests it is not fully adequate, and a model incorporating seasonality (e.g., SARIMA) would likely perform better.

The diagnostic plots (@fig-plot31) for the ARMA(0,1) model reveal its performance and limitations. The "Standardized Residuals" plot shows residuals fluctuating around zero with no clear trend over time, indicating the model captures the mean structure adequately, though occasional residuals exceed ±2, suggesting potential outliers or unmodelled variability. The "ACF of Residuals" plot displays significant spikes at lags around 0.5, 1.0, and 1.5 (approximately 6, 12, and 18 months), highlighting a persistent seasonal pattern (annual cycle) that the model fails to capture, as it lacks seasonal components. The "p-values for Ljung-Box statistic" plot shows p-values consistently below 0.05 for lags 1 to 10, rejecting the null hypothesis of no autocorrelation in the residuals, which confirms the presence of unmodelled structure, primarily due to seasonality. Overall, while the ARMA(0,1) model fits the mean reasonably well, its inability to account for the seasonal autocorrelation indicates it is not fully adequate, suggesting a model with seasonal components (e.g., SARIMA) would be more appropriate.

### Comments

The diagnostic plots ( @fig-plot32) for the ARMA(1,1) model highlight both its strengths and shortcomings. The Standardized Residuals plot shows that residuals fluctuate around zero without a clear trend, indicating the model effectively captures the mean. However, a few residuals lie beyond ±2, suggesting possible outliers or unexplained variability. The ACF of Residuals reveals prominent spikes at lags around 0.5, 1.0, and 1.5 years (roughly 6, 12, and 18 months), indicating a seasonal pattern specifically an annual cycle that the model does not capture, likely due to the exclusion of seasonal terms as specified in the task. The Ljung-Box p-values remain below 0.05 across lags 1 to 10, leading to rejection of the hypothesis of no autocorrelation and pointing to residual autocorrelation, primarily from seasonality. In summary, the ARMA(1,1) model sufficiently captures the overall mean behaviour of the series, but its failure to model the seasonal autocorrelation suggests it is incomplete. A more appropriate model would include seasonal elements, such as a SARIMA model, to better reflect the underlying structure.

### ARIMA Models

#### Differencing plot

```{r,fig.cap='ACF/PACF of First Difference plots', fig-plot33,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE}
moc.ts.diff <- diff(moc.ts.train, lag = 1)
par(mfrow=c(1,2),mar=c(4,4,3,2))
acf(moc.ts.diff, main = "ACF of First Difference")
pacf(moc.ts.diff, main = "PACF of First Difference")

```

### Comments

The ACF and PACF plots of the first-differenced AMOC strength data (from January 2017 to June 2022) offer valuable insights for selecting an appropriate ARIMA model without seasonal terms (@fig-plot33). The ACF of the First Difference plot shows a pronounced negative spike at lag 1 (approximately -0.5), followed by smaller spikes at lags corresponding to 6, 12, and 18 months. While these later spikes fall within the confidence bounds, they hint at a lingering seasonal pattern. The significant lag 1 spike suggests that a moving average component of order 1 (MA(1)) may be appropriate. Similarly, the PACF of the First Difference plot features a notable negative spike at lag 1 (around -0.4), along with minor spikes at seasonal intervals (also within the bounds), implying that an autoregressive component of order 1 (AR(1)) might also be suitable. Taken together, these plots suggest that an ARIMA(1,1,1) model is a reasonable fit for the data after differencing. However, the presence of residual seasonal signals suggests that incorporating seasonal components, such as in a SARIMA model, could further improve model performance in a more detailed analysis.

### Comments

The ARIMA(0,1,1) model shows strong performance for the AMOC strength data from January 2017 to June 2022 (@tbl-table14). The MA(1) coefficient is -0.899 with a small standard error, indicating a significant negative error correction. The AIC (327.75) is the lowest, suggesting the best overall model fit. While the model does not address seasonality, it outperforms others in terms of simplicity and accuracy.

```{r,fig.cap='Diagnostic plots', fig-plot35,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE}
# residuals check
par(mfrow=c(1,2),mar=c(4,4,3.5,4))
tsdiag(arima011.b)
```

### Comments

The diagnostic plots for the ARIMA(0,1,1) model fitted to the AMOC strength data from 2017 to 2022 reveal key insights into its residuals (@fig-plot35). The standardized residuals plot shows no clear trend or significant outliers, fluctuating around zero, suggesting the model captures the data's level well after differencing. The ACF (Autocorrelation Function) of residuals indicates no significant autocorrelation beyond the first lag, with all autocorrelations falling within the confidence bounds (approximately ±0.1), implying the MA(1) term adequately accounts for short-term dependencies. The p-values for the Ljung-Box statistic, all above 0.05 up to lag 10, further confirm the absence of significant residual autocorrelation, supporting the model's adequacy for the data. Overall, these diagnostics suggest that the ARIMA(0,1,1) model is appropriately specified, though it lacks seasonal components, which may limit its ability to capture longer-term patterns in the AMOC strength time series.

### Comments

The diagnostic plots (@fig-plot36) for the ARIMA(1,1,1) model fitted to AMOC strength data (January 2017 to June 2022) highlight both strengths and limitations. The Standardized Residuals fluctuate around zero without a clear trend, indicating a good fit to the mean, though a few exceed ±2, suggesting some unexplained variation. The ACF of Residuals shows clear spikes at lags 0.5, 1.0, and 1.5 (6, 12, and 18 months), pointing to not modelled seasonality. Additionally, Ljung-Box p-values remain below 0.05 across all lags, confirming significant residual autocorrelation. While the model performs reasonably well based on its AIC (329.49), the persistent seasonal structure in the residuals indicates that ARIMA(1,1,1) is not sufficient. A SARIMA model would likely provide a better fit by capturing this seasonality.

## (c) Quarterly Means of AMOC

```{r,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE}
# Convert monthly data to quarterly means
moc.ts.quarterly.train <- aggregate(moc.ts.train, nfrequency = 4, FUN = mean)

# Verify the quarterly time series
#print(moc.ts.quarterly.train)

```

```{r,fig.cap='Quarterly Average of (AMOC) Jan 2017-Jun 2022', fig-plot37,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE}

# Plot with autoplot and scale_x_date

```

### Comments

The plot of quarterly AMOC strength (@fig-plot37) shows values fluctuating between 14 and 20, with no clear trend but a visible annual cycle (period = 4 quarters). Peaks typically occur in Q2 or Q3 (e.g., mid-2018, mid-2019, mid-2021), while troughs appear around Q4 or Q1 (e.g., early 2018, late 2019), indicating strong seasonality. The series appears stationary overall, as the mean level hovers around 16–17 without a consistent upward or downward trend, though variability suggests potential non-stationarity in variance. This supports the need for a SARIMA model with seasonal differencing ($D$=1, period = 4) to capture the annual cycle, and possibly a non-seasonal difference ($d$=1) if stationarity is not confirmed by an ADF test.

```{r,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE,tab.cap='ADF Test for Quarterly AMOC Strength',tbl-table17}

library(tseries)
adf.test(moc.ts.quarterly.train)

# Load the gt library
library(gt)

# Create data frame for ADF test results
adf_data <- data.frame(
  Parameter = c("Dickey-Fuller", "Lag order", "p-value"),
  Value = c(-4.6409, 2, 0.01)
)

# Create the table with gt
adf_table <- gt(data = adf_data, rowname_col = "Parameter") %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Augmented Dickey-Fuller Test for Quarterly AMOC Strength"
  ) %>%
  cols_label(
    Value = "Value"
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = "Value",
    rows = c(1, 3),  # Dickey-Fuller and p-value
    decimals = 3
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = "Value",
    rows = 2,  # Lag order
    decimals = 0
  ) %>%
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = "Alternative Hypothesis: Stationary"
  )

# Display the table
adf_table
```

### Comments

The ADF test for the quarterly AMOC strength data ( @tbl-table17) yields a Dickey-Fuller statistic of -4.641 with a lag order of 2 and a p-value of 0.010. Since the p-value is below 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis of a unit root, indicating that the series is stationary. This implies that non-seasonal differencing (𝑑 = 0) is not required for ARIMA or SARIMA modelling. However, the clear annual seasonality observed in the time series (with a period of 4) suggests that seasonal differencing (𝐷 = 1) may still be necessary in a SARIMA model to adequately capture the cyclical behaviour.

```{r,fig.cap='ACF/PACF of Quarterly AMOC Strength',fig-plot38,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE}
# ACF and PACF plots
par(mfrow = c(1, 2),mar=c(4,4,2,1))
acf(moc.ts.quarterly.train, main = "ACF of Quarterly \n AMOC Strength")
pacf(moc.ts.quarterly.train, main = "PACF of Quarterly \n AMOC Strength")

```

### Comments

The ACF and PACF plots (@fig-plot38) for the quarterly AMOC strength data provide insights into its structure. The ACF plot shows no significant spikes, with all values within the confidence bounds (±0.4), indicating no strong autocorrelation or slow decay, which aligns with the ADF test (p-value = 0.01) confirming stationarity. However, the lack of clear seasonal spikes at lags 4, 8, etc., suggests that the annual cycle (period = 4) seen in the time series plot may be less pronounced in the autocorrelation structure, possibly due to the small sample size (22 quarters). The PACF plot also shows no significant spikes, with values within ±0.4, suggesting no clear AR component. Given stationarity ($d$=0), but considering the visible seasonality in the time series plot, a SARIMA model with seasonal differencing ($D$=1, period = 4) and minimal non-seasonal components (e.g., SARIMA(0,0,0)(0,1,1)\[4\]) may be appropriate to capture the annual cycle.

### ARMA and SARIMA Models

The time series plot shows an annual cycle, so we will use a SARIMA model with $D$=1, period = 4. Additionally, the ACF and PACF plots for the quarterly data showed no significant spikes at non-seasonal lags (e.g., lag 1, 2, 3), all within the confidence bounds (±0.4). This strongly suggests that there’s no need for non-seasonal AR ($𝑝$) or MA ($q$) terms, as there’s no clear non-seasonal autocorrelation or error structure to model.

```{r,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE}
                       seasonal = list(order = c(0, 1, 1), period = 4))
#sarima000_011
```

```{r,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE,tab.cap='Comparison of Fitted Models for Quarterly AMOC Strength (Jan-2017 to Jun-2022',tbl-table18}
library(gt)
library(tidyverse)

# Function to extract coefficients from a model
extract_coefficients <- function(model, model_name) {
  coefs <- data.frame(
    Parameter = names(model$coef),
    Estimate = model$coef,
    Std_Error = sqrt(diag(model$var.coef))
  )
  coefs$Model <- model_name
  coefs
}

# Function to extract fit statistics
extract_fit_stats <- function(model, model_name) {
  data.frame(
    Model = model_name,
    Sigma2 = model$sigma2,
    Log_Likelihood = model$loglik,
    AIC = model$aic
  )
}

# Extract all coefficients

  extract_coefficients(arma10, "ARMA(1,0)"),
  extract_coefficients(arma01, "ARMA(0,1)"),

  extract_coefficients(sarima000_011, "SARIMA(0,0,0)(0,1,1)[4]")
) %>% 
  mutate(Parameter = case_when(
    Parameter == "ar1" ~ "ar1",
    Parameter == "ma1" ~ "ma1",
    Parameter == "intercept" ~ "intercept",

  ))

# Extract all fit statistics

  extract_fit_stats(arma10, "ARMA(1,0)"),

)

# Create coefficients table

  )

# Create fit statistics table

  tab_spanner(

  ) %>%
```

### Comments

The tables ( @tbl-table18, @tbl-table19) compare ARMA and SARIMA models fitted to the quarterly AMOC strength data. Both ARMA(1,0) (AIC = 92.76) and ARMA(0,1) (AIC = 93.09) have non-significant coefficients, indicating weak performance and failure to capture the seasonal pattern. ARMA(1,1) performs worse (AIC = 94.31) with large standard errors, suggesting parameter instability. In contrast, the SARIMA(0,0,0)(0,1,1)\[4\] model achieves the lowest AIC (79.71) and includes a seasonal MA(1) term (sma1 = -0.367, s.e. = 0.295), effectively capturing the annual cycle. These results show that the SARIMA model provides the best fit by addressing the seasonality present in the data, while the ARMA models fall short.


### Comments

The diagnostic plots for the SARIMA(0,0,0)(0,1,1)[4] model demonstrate that the "Standardized Residuals" plot shows residuals fluctuating around zero with no clear trend, and all are within ±2.5, indicating no obvious outliers or not modelled patterns ( @fig-plot39). The "ACF of Residuals" plot has no significant spikes (all within ±0.4), suggesting no residual autocorrelation, meaning the model captures the data’s structure well. The "p-values for Ljung-Box statistic" are all above 0.05 (around 0.8), failing to reject the null hypothesis of no autocorrelation in the residuals, further confirming the model’s adequacy. Overall, the SARIMA(0,0,0)(0,1,1)[4] model effectively captures the annual cycle and stationarity of the data, with no significant residual patterns, making it a suitable fit for the quarterly dataset.

## (d) Dynamic Linear Model with a linear trend and a seasonal component to Monthly dataset

### Monthly DLM

```{r,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE}
# Defining the DLM Model
library(dlm)
build_dlm_monthly <- function(par) {
  dlmModPoly(order = 2, dV = exp(par[1]), 
             dW = c(exp(par[2]), exp(par[3]))) + 
  dlmModSeas(frequency = 12, dV = 0, 
             dW = rep(exp(par[4]), 11))
}

# Optimising the Variances
## This step uses maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) 
# to find the optimal values of par that best fit the data
dlm_fit_monthly <- dlmMLE(y = as.numeric(moc.ts.train), 
                          parm = c(0, 0, 0, 0), build = build_dlm_monthly)

# fit DLM model
dlm_model_monthly <- build_dlm_monthly(dlm_fit_monthly$par)


# Filter the model to get fitted values and residuals
dlm_filtered_monthly <- dlmFilter(y = as.numeric(moc.ts.train), 
                                  mod = dlm_model_monthly)

# Smooth the model to get state estimates
dlm_smoothed_monthly <- dlmSmooth(dlm_filtered_monthly)

```

```{r,message=TRUE,warning=FALSE}
# Compute the negative log-likelihood
neg_log_lik_monthly <- dlmLL(y = as.numeric(moc.ts.train), 
                             mod = dlm_model_monthly)

# Compute the actual log-likelihood
log_lik_monthly <- -neg_log_lik_monthly

# Compute the number of parameters (k)
# - Variances: 4 (V, W_level, W_slope, W_seas)
k <- 4

# Compute AIC
aic_monthly <- -2 * log_lik_monthly + 2 * k
cat("Log-Likelihood for Monthly DLM:", log_lik_monthly, "\n")
cat("AIC for Monthly DLM:", aic_monthly, "\n")
```

```{r,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE}
# Defining the DLM Model
library(dlm)
build_dlm_quarterly <- function(par) {
  dlmModPoly(order = 2, dV = exp(par[1]), dW = c(exp(par[2]), exp(par[3]))) + 
  dlmModSeas(frequency = 4, dV = 0, dW = rep(exp(par[4]), 3))
}

# Optimising the Variances
## This step uses maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) 
# to find the optimal values of par that best fit the data
dlm_fit_quarterly <- dlmMLE(y = as.numeric(moc.ts.quarterly.train), 
                            parm = c(0, 0, 0, 0), 
                            build = build_dlm_quarterly)

# fit DLM model
dlm_model_quarterly <- build_dlm_quarterly(dlm_fit_quarterly$par)


# Filter the model to get fitted values and residuals
dlm_filtered_quarterly <- dlmFilter(y = as.numeric(moc.ts.quarterly.train),
                                    mod = dlm_model_quarterly)

# Smooth the model to get state estimates
dlm_smoothed_quarterly <- dlmSmooth(dlm_filtered_quarterly)
```

```{r}
# Compute the negative log-likelihood
neg_log_lik_quarterly <- dlmLL(y = as.numeric(moc.ts.quarterly.train), 
                               mod = dlm_model_quarterly)

# Compute the actual log-likelihood
log_lik_quarterly <- -neg_log_lik_quarterly

# Compute the number of parameters (k)
# - Variances: 4 (V, W_level, W_slope, W_seas)
k <- 4

# Compute AIC
aic_quarterly <- -2 * log_lik_quarterly + 2 * k
cat("Log-Likelihood for Quarterly DLM:", log_lik_quarterly, "\n")
cat("AIC for Quarterly DLM:", aic_quarterly, "\n")
```

#### Comments

The AIC(134.5713) for the quarterly DLM is the lowest, making it the best model compared to the monthly DLM with AIC of 406.8182.

## (e) Forecast of the best models from b to d

The best model for the monthly data (training set Jan 2017 to Jun 2022) is ARIMA(0,1,1). While for the quarterly data (training set 2017 to 2022), the best model is SARIMA(0,0,0)(0,1,1)\[4\]. For the DLM models, quarterly one is the best over monthly DLM.

#### Forecast of the next 8 months using the best models

```{r,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE}
# Forecast of the next 8 months for the arima011
library(forecast)
arima_forecast_monthly <- forecast(arima011.b, h=8)
```

```{r,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE}
# Forecast the next 8 months for the sarima000_011
library(forecast)
sarima_forecast_quarterly <- forecast(sarima000_011, h=2)
```

```{r,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE}
# Forecast the next 8 months for the monthly DLM
library(forecast)
dlm_forecast_monthly <- dlmForecast(dlm_filtered_monthly, nAhead = 8)

### Compute standard deviations for confidence intervals
sqrtR.monthly <- sapply(dlm_forecast_monthly$R, function(x)sqrt(x[1,1]))

# Compute 95% confidence intervals
pl.month <- dlm_forecast_monthly$a[,1] + 
                    qnorm(0.025, sd = sqrtR.monthly)

pu.month <- dlm_forecast_monthly$a[,1] + 
                    qnorm(0.975, sd = sqrtR.monthly)


# Convert forecast vectors to ts objects with correct time indices
# Forecasts are for Jul 2022 (2022.5) to Feb 2023 (2023.0833), frequency = 12

forecast_dates <- seq(from = 2022 + 6/12, to = 2023 + 1/12,
                      length.out = 8)

forecast_level_ts <- ts(dlm_forecast_monthly$a[,1], 
                        start = c(2022, 7), frequency = 12)

forecast_mean_ts <- ts(dlm_forecast_monthly$f, 
                       start = c(2022, 7), frequency = 12)

 # Compute 95% confidence intervals
pl_month_ts <- ts(pl.month, start = c(2022, 7), frequency = 12)
pu_month_ts <- ts(pu.month, start = c(2022, 7), frequency = 12)

# Combine with training data using ts.union
x.month <- ts.union(
  window(moc.ts.train, start = c(2017, 1)),
  forecast_level_ts,
  forecast_mean_ts,
  pl_month_ts,
  pu_month_ts
)
```

```{r,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE}

### Compute standard deviations for confidence intervals

# Compute 95% confidence intervals
pl.quarterly <- dlm_forecast_quarterly$a[,1] + 
                    qnorm(0.025, sd = sqrtR.quarterly)

pu.quarterly <- dlm_forecast_quarterly$a[,1] +

                      start = c(2022, 3), frequency = 4)
```

